channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: India and China are exploring a framework for Chinese investment ahead of Xi Jinping's visit for the BRICS summit on 12-13 September, as foreign investors withdraw money from Indian markets and Indian ministers tour abroad to court capital.
item.description:
India and China are discussing a framework to make business-to-business contact and Chinese investment easier, with a focus on speeding up capital flows, as diplomatic relations warm. People familiar with the talks say Beijing may present an investment package for India during Xi Jinping's visit for the BRICS summit on 12-13 September, possibly including a special economic zone with easier sea access. Reported elements include a push for Chinese electric vehicles, among them BYD, to enter the Indian market, and a proposal for third-country exports from an export-processing zone in India built with Chinese funding. The context is a weaker investment position. Foreign investors have withdrawn money from Indian equities and bonds this year, with relatively high domestic valuations and AI and semiconductor investment elsewhere drawing capital away. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman is on a nine-day visit to Canada and the United States and Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal is in Japan, both presenting India as an investment destination. Indian industry is separately pressing for changes to the India-Japan trade agreement: the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry says the trade deficit has widened since it was signed, and exporters cite Japanese certification requirements and procurement practices as barriers.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

India is one of the faster-growing markets for construction and industrial ACS products, so how it attracts manufacturing investment shapes where that demand forms. Chinese investment in Indian manufacturing, if it proceeds, could add local capacity in vehicles and electronics, both ACS-consuming sectors, and would bring Chinese suppliers into a market where several Western producers have been building positions. The proposals are at an early stage and India has restricted Chinese investment since 2020, so the September visit is better read as a signal of direction than as a settled outcome. The retreat of portfolio investors is a separate matter that mainly affects financing conditions rather than industrial demand. Considerations include following what is announced around 12-13 September, and watching whether an India-Japan review changes certification requirements, which affect market access for chemical and coating products as well as for the goods cited.

The Economic Times | The Hindu BusinessLine | The Times of India | New Indian Express

item.title: A glacier collapse on the Nepal-Tibet border triggered a flash flood that has killed at least 160 people, left 403 tourists unaccounted for, hit about 748 MW of hydropower capacity and cut a main China-Nepal trade crossing.
item.description:
A large ice-and-rock avalanche in the Himalayas on 26 August blocked the Lhende Khola, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi on the Nepal-Tibet border, then released the impounded water and debris downstream. Preliminary analysis by the National Remote Sensing Centre of India's space agency ISRO, using satellite images taken the same day, traces the sequence to a glacier collapse in which close to two-thirds of the glacier body detached. The US Geological Survey found no earthquake in the area, and scientists are still reconstructing the order of events. Nepali police had recovered at least 160 bodies by 26 August, and Nepal's tourism ministry listed 403 tourists as unaccounted for, including 341 foreign nationals; Chinese authorities reported at least three deaths on the Tibet side. Officials in both countries expect the toll to rise. The economic damage is concentrated in energy and trade. Nepal's insurance authority reported damage affecting about 13 hydropower projects, roughly 354 MW already producing and 394 MW under construction. The Nepal Stock Exchange fell, its hydropower sub-index down 2.84%. The Rasuwagadhi-Gyirong customs crossing was damaged; more than 6,500 Chinese electric cars, jeeps, vans and minibuses entered Nepal through it in 2025-26, alongside electronics, garments and footwear.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Direct exposure for ACS producers is limited: Nepal is a small market and the affected corridor carries mainly consumer goods and vehicles. Two second-order points may still be relevant. The first is route concentration — a single crossing carried a large share of one country's imports from China, and its loss shows how quickly a land corridor can be removed from a supply chain; comparable single-point dependencies exist on other overland routes used for Asian sourcing. The second is the hazard type. A glacier collapse with no earthquake trigger, in a range that is warming quickly, is the kind of event insurers and lenders are beginning to price into infrastructure and hydropower projects, which could raise costs for construction and energy assets in mountain regions over time. Considerations include checking whether any inbound or outbound flows depend on a single land crossing, and following how physical-climate risk assessments treat glacial hazards in project financing.

BBC News | Dawn | The Statesman | The Times of India | The Times of India | Al Jazeera

item.title: The US Justice Department seized the domains behind two Chinese state-linked hacking platforms that had breached federal agencies since at least 2018, and Trump signed an emergency order barring some foreign-made electrical grid equipment.
item.description:
On 26 August the US Justice Department said it had disrupted a Chinese state-linked hacking operation and seized the domains behind two platforms, QScan and QTRouter, reported to be operated by Nanjing Xinjiuwei Network Technology. The group is said to have been working to breach US critical infrastructure and sensitive federal networks since at least 2018. Named victims include the Senate, the Federal Reserve, NASA, the Justice Department itself, the National Institutes of Health, the Department of Health and Human Services and the Department of Energy, together with four unnamed companies in the United States and South Korea. Beijing routinely rejects responsibility for such activity. The same day, Trump signed an emergency order barring the purchase or installation of certain foreign-made bulk-power system electrical equipment and related software. The order rests on a national emergency declaration under two federal laws and gives the Energy Department 120 days to publish implementing regulations; Energy Secretary Chris Wright was asked to identify further changes addressing risks in grid equipment. Reports note the measure could favour domestic manufacturers of electrical equipment.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Both measures point the same way: the US is treating foreign-supplied industrial technology and long-running network access as infrastructure risks and is acting on both. For chemical and ACS producers the nearer relevance is operational. Sites with process-control and building-management systems, and the energy assets connected to them, fall into the same target category as the agencies named here, and a group active since 2018 indicates dwell times measured in years rather than weeks. The grid-equipment order adds a procurement dimension: once the Energy Department publishes rules within 120 days, some electrical equipment for US sites may need to be sourced differently, with possible effects on lead times and cost. Considerations include reviewing detection coverage on operational-technology networks rather than only on office IT, asking suppliers of electrical and control equipment about their exposure to the coming rules, and allowing for possible equipment lead-time changes in US capital projects.

The Economic Times | The Express Tribune | LiveMint

item.title: Taiwan set out a six-year TWD 44.2 billion plan to build a drone industry alongside a TWD 210 billion procurement bill, as France and Germany reported gaps in their own defences against cheap drones.
item.description:
Taiwan set out a six-year plan worth TWD 44.2 billion to build a domestic drone industry, with the budget spread evenly across the period and organised around four strands: reviewing regulation, creating demand, technology and international cooperation, and forming industry clusters. Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim, who presented the plan, said development is held back by regulatory limits and a shortage of test airspace; the Executive Yuan has designated 18 test areas and is shortening application times, and the shutdown of the National Communications Commission, which manages radio spectrum, has added pressure. A separate draft act would allocate up to TWD 210 billion for coastal surveillance drones, coastal attack drones and small unmanned boats. Legislators have not agreed a common text across 14 competing versions; the Legislative Yuan moved its session forward to 27 August, ahead of possible typhoon closures, to attempt a third reading. In Europe the position is defensive. A senior French general warned that France is not ready to counter cheap, mass-produced drones, noting that the air force has used costly missiles against low-cost Iranian-made drones aimed at Gulf states. The German aviation association BDL put drone-related business interruption at EUR 60 million in 2025, with follow-on costs taking the total to EUR 160 million, and said eight German airports are due to receive counter-drone equipment.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Drone and counter-drone programmes are a growing source of demand for materials the ACS sector supplies: lightweight structural bonding, potting and encapsulation for electronics, conformal coatings and protective finishes. Taiwan's plan is notable for pairing procurement with cluster formation, which suggests a supply chain built largely on the island and served by suppliers able to qualify locally. European spending appears to be moving towards detection and defence systems around airports and military sites rather than towards large-scale airframe production, which points to a different and smaller materials opportunity. The unresolved legislation in Taipei is a reminder that announced budgets are not yet committed spending. Points to consider include tracking whether the TWD 210 billion procurement act passes and what it specifies, and assessing qualification requirements for defence and aviation applications, which are typically long and may need to be started well before the demand appears.

Commercial Times | Commercial Times | Commercial Times | Politico Europe | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung

item.title: China had about 15 million units of excess vehicle production capacity in 2025, roughly a year of US car sales, giving its manufacturers a standing reason to export, as North American and UK production declined.
item.description:
An analysis by the Center for Automotive Research puts China's excess vehicle production capacity at about 15 million units in 2025, roughly equal to a full year of US car sales. Chinese brands' sales have tripled in Western Europe and risen sevenfold in other markets since 2020; in Mexico they reached 14.5% of the market in 2025, from under 1% in 2020. Production in the established markets moved the other way. The Omdia outlook cited by the Alliance for Automotive Innovation expects North American light-vehicle output to fall 0.9% year on year to 11.857 million units in the first nine months of 2026, with a 1.3% decline in the third quarter. In the United Kingdom, the SMMT reported July output down 11.6% year on year, which it attributed to earlier summer maintenance shutdowns and weaker exports, with production of electric and hybrid models up 6.8%. German premium manufacturers, facing lower market shares in China and tariffs in the US, are reported to be looking harder at Indonesia, Thailand, India, Australia, Brazil and Argentina. Wan Gang, honorary chairman of the China Association for Science and Technology, argued that production capacity alone is a poor measure of overcapacity and that demand potential should be assessed alongside it.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Vehicle assembly is one of the largest single end-markets for industrial adhesives, sealants and coatings, so where vehicles are built matters to ACS suppliers as much as how many are built. Output is falling in North America and the United Kingdom, and Chinese capacity remains well above domestic demand. Taken together these point to a gradual shift in where ACS volume sits — towards Chinese plants and towards the export markets Chinese brands are entering. Serving that volume usually means competing with local formulators close to those plants. Wan Gang's objection is a reminder that capacity figures alone do not establish oversupply, so the export trend may be better tracked through registration and shipment data than through capacity estimates. Considerations include reviewing regional ACS capacity against where vehicle assembly is growing, and watching Chinese brand share in Europe, Mexico and Southeast Asia as an indicator of where automotive ACS demand may migrate.

Axios | Alliance for Automotive Innovation | MarketScreener | Handelsblatt | Chinatimes

item.title: China's industry ministry set its 2026-2030 agenda, naming integrated circuits, aerospace, biomedicine, the low-altitude economy, energy storage and intelligent robots as pillar industries, with 6G, quantum, fusion and hydrogen as longer-term bets.
item.description:
At a State Council briefing on 26 August, Vice Minister of Industry and Information Technology Xin Guobin set out the industrial agenda for the 15th Five-Year Plan period, 2026 to 2030. Beijing will work to build a group of emerging pillar industries: integrated circuits, aerospace, biomedicine, the low-altitude economy — commercial activity using drones and small aircraft in low airspace — new energy storage and intelligent robots. A second group is framed as future industries and longer-term growth points: sixth-generation mobile communications, quantum technology, nuclear fusion, hydrogen energy, biomanufacturing, brain-computer interfaces and embodied intelligence, meaning AI systems that act in the physical world. The ministry said it has drafted close to 200 key AI standards and plans 500 zero-carbon factories over the period, and that commercialising AI in manufacturing is a priority. A separate five-year plan covers intelligent connected and new-energy vehicles, with stated aims of improving autonomous-driving safety, battery durability and low-temperature performance, and adjusting insurance and repair costs to raise buyer confidence. Over the previous plan period, NEV sales rose from 1.367 million to 16.49 million units, taking their share of new-car sales from 5.4% to 47.9%.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Several of the named pillar industries are ACS-intensive: integrated circuits, aerospace, energy storage, robots and electric vehicles all use structural adhesives, encapsulants, thermal-interface materials, conformal coatings and specialty sealants. A stated five-year commitment gives an indication of where Chinese demand for these chemistries is likely to concentrate, and where local formulators will be encouraged to serve it. The 500 zero-carbon factories and the near-200 AI standards suggest product carbon data and digital documentation may become conditions of supply into these chains, pointing in a similar direction to European requirements though under different rules. Things that may be worth considering include reviewing which parts of the ACS portfolio align with the named pillar industries, assessing whether serving them would require local formulation and technical service, and monitoring how the zero-carbon factory programme defines its requirements, since that would shape what suppliers are asked to document.

South China Morning Post | Xinhua | China Daily | Beijing Daily | Chinatimes

item.title: Germany's housing shortage stood at 1.35 million units at the end of 2025 and completions are heading for a 15-year low, which one study estimates has cost about EUR 26.9 billion in construction revenue and 0.6 percentage points of GDP.
item.description:
The Bau-Monitor 2026, prepared by the Pestel Institute for the German Building Materials Trade Association, puts the housing shortage at 1.35 million units at the end of 2025, down slightly from about 1.4 million in the two preceding years. It reports that 84,600 fewer homes were completed in 2025 than two years earlier, equal to more than nine million square metres of floor space, with the largest falls in Bavaria (18,750 fewer), Baden-Wuerttemberg (12,270) and North Rhine-Westphalia (10,720). The study estimates the decline cost the construction sector about EUR 26.9 billion in revenue over two years, reduced GDP by roughly 0.6 percentage points and cut tax revenue by around EUR 7 billion. The Ifo Institute expects about 185,000 completions this year, which would be the lowest in 15 years, against an estimated need of at least 300,000 a year; 206,600 homes were completed in 2025. The picture is not uniformly negative. Construction orders and building permits have been rising this year, and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said the housing sector is developing well. Completions lag orders and permits by a year or more, so both readings can hold at the same time.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Residential construction is one of the larger end-markets for adhesives, sealants, tile adhesives, floor systems and architectural coatings, so completion volumes bear directly on ACS demand in Germany. A projected 185,000 completions against a stated need of 300,000 points to a gap that policy has not yet closed, and the estimated 0.6 percentage point drag suggests the shortfall is large enough to affect the wider recovery described in the German export insight in this alert. The rise in orders and permits is the more forward-looking series and could lift completions from 2027, so near-term and medium-term signals may point in different directions. Considerations include separating renovation and refurbishment demand, which is less tied to completions, from new-build demand when setting German volume assumptions, and treating permits and orders rather than completions as the early indicator for when new-build ACS volumes might recover.

Anadolu Agency | Handelsblatt | Wallstreet:online

item.title: German export expectations jumped to their highest level since February 2022 and Chancellor Merz said three years of recession are behind the country, though the Ifo survey shows the improvement is uneven across industries.
item.description:
The Ifo Institute's export expectations index for German manufacturing rose to 9.6 points in August from minus 2.8 in July, the highest reading since February 2022. Ifo economist Klaus Wohlrabe said exports to the European Union are strong while shipments to China remain sluggish. The improvement is not spread evenly: makers of electrical equipment, data-processing equipment and electronic and optical products are the most optimistic, helped by digitalisation and AI investment, and carmakers and metal-product manufacturers have also turned more positive, while the paper industry and metal production and processing expect their exports to decline. After a two-day cabinet retreat at Schloss Neuhardenberg, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said three years of recession are behind Germany, that the economy is growing again and that 2027 forecasts are being revised up; Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil pointed to rising orders. Official data show GDP growth of 0.3% to 0.4% for three consecutive quarters, driven in the first half by exports, a pace close to the average since 2010. Industry associations are still pressing for change: Audi, BMW, Mercedes-Benz and the metal and electrical employers' associations wrote to the government last week calling for faster reform, and the chemical industry association VCI called this week for a signal on growth.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Germany is the largest European market for industrial ACS products, so export sentiment among its manufacturers is a reasonable leading indicator for industrial adhesive and coating volumes. The composition of the survey is the more useful part: electronics, data-processing equipment and vehicles are ACS-intensive and are turning positive, while paper and metal processing, also ACS end-markets, expect further declines. Any recovery in demand may therefore arrive unevenly across product portfolios rather than as a general lift. Three quarters of growth at 0.3% to 0.4% is a return to the long-run average rather than a strong upswing, so reading the Chancellor's assessment as confirmation of a broad recovery may go beyond what the data show. Points to consider include tracking the Ifo sub-sector readings alongside order intake by end-market, and watching whether the reform requests from the VCI and the automotive associations translate into measures on energy costs, which remain a large part of the German cost gap.

MarketScreener | WirtschaftsWoche | Sueddeutsche Zeitung | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Les Echos | Tagesschau

item.title: Trump and Xi are expected to meet at the White House on 24 September, with Washington reported to be preparing an additional 7.5% tariff on Chinese goods beforehand and weighing how to handle a stalled USD 14 billion arms package for Taiwan.
item.description:
The meeting is now expected at the White House on 24 September, with tariffs, Taiwan, geopolitics and artificial intelligence on the agenda and both sides looking to extend the existing trade arrangement. Media reports say the administration expects to impose an additional 7.5% tariff on Chinese goods before the meeting, applied on an "excess manufacturing capacity" rationale, which would take the second-term tariff rate on Chinese goods to about 20% and closer to the ceiling agreed earlier. Since March, Washington has used Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 — the provision allowing action against trade practices judged unfair — to open overcapacity investigations into more than ten trading partners. Reports indicate the 7.5% rate is not final and could still be adjusted before any announcement. On Taiwan, officials in Taipei expect Washington to break a stalled USD 14 billion arms package into smaller cases to avoid raising tension before the summit. Their concern is wider than one package: a reduction in joint exercises with South Korea and the shift of US military resources to the Middle East have left several Asian partners less certain about American security commitments.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The summit gives trade policy toward China a fixed date to cluster around, which planning has lacked. If the additional 7.5% tariff is applied first, it would raise landed costs for Chinese-origin inputs and finished goods entering the US, including chemical intermediates and products made with them, and could draw Chinese countermeasures. A tariff imposed shortly before a negotiation may also prove reversible, so treating it as permanent could be as costly as ignoring it. Considerations include identifying which purchased inputs would fall under an overcapacity tariff line, keeping pricing decisions provisional until after 24 September, and following whether the current arrangement is extended, since that would set much of the tariff environment for 2027. The security signals matter more for longer-term footprint decisions in East Asia than for near-term cost.

Commercial Times | Chinatimes | Chinatimes | South China Morning Post

item.title: US inflation on the Federal Reserve's preferred measure rose to 3.7% in July, slightly above forecast, and second-quarter growth was confirmed at 1.5%, lifting market odds of a September rate rise from about 36% to about 44%.
item.description:
Two releases on 26 August moved the US rate outlook. The personal consumption expenditures price index, the gauge the Federal Reserve targets, rose 3.7% in the year to July, against the 3.6% economists expected; the core reading, which excludes food and energy, held at 3.3% with a 0.2% monthly rise. The Commerce Department confirmed second-quarter growth at a 1.5% annualised pace, down from 2.1% in the first quarter. The detail was firmer than the headline: consumer spending ran at 3.4%, up from 0.5%, business investment was revised up to 8.5%, and imports rose at a 12.5% pace, partly on shipments of chips and other equipment supporting artificial-intelligence investment. Futures markets moved the probability of a rise at the 15-16 September meeting from about 36% to about 44%. Attention now turns to Jackson Hole, where Kevin Warsh gives his first major speech as Fed chair. In the euro area, ECB Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel said rates will need to rise further, citing the Middle East conflict and stronger-than-expected euro-area growth. The fiscal backdrop is heavier: US federal debt passed USD 40 trillion this month and the 30-year Treasury yield reached 5.33%, its highest since 2007.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Policy rates and long-term yields both reach ACS end-markets through construction and durable-goods demand, and reach the sector directly through financing costs. A September rise is not yet the market's base case at roughly 44%, so the more useful signal may be direction: inflation is not returning to target, and two of the largest central banks are being pushed the same way, in part by energy costs. Long yields near 2007 levels raise the hurdle on capital projects and on housing, which could weigh on building activity into 2027. Morgan Stanley argues the size of the debt is not in itself the trigger, and that the risk to watch is investors reallocating away from equities if yields stay high. Things that may be worth considering include stress-testing capital-expenditure plans against a higher-for-longer rate path, revisiting US construction and automotive volume assumptions, and following Warsh's Jackson Hole remarks for a first read on how the new chair frames the trade-off.

The Globe and Mail | The Economic Times | MarketScreener | Los Angeles Times | Bloomberg | Cinco Dias | Cnyes

item.title: Six months of war have produced 68 merchant-ship accidents in the Strait of Hormuz, a 4% rise in Britain's household energy price cap and a Japanese plan to subsidise crude that avoids the strait.
item.description:
The costs are now visible in freight, bills and government policy. The International Maritime Organization counted 68 merchant-ship accidents in the Strait of Hormuz over six months of conflict, about one every 2.6 days, with at least 20 seafarers or port workers killed, 35 injured and one missing; about half involved tankers, and the UK Maritime Trade Operations office in Dubai classed 47 of them as attacks. In Britain, the regulator Ofgem will raise the domestic energy price cap — the maximum per-unit price suppliers may charge households on variable tariffs — by 4%, or GBP 60, to GBP 1,723 from October, affecting around 22 million households, after wholesale UK gas prices more than doubled since US military action began on 28 February. Japan published a plan to reduce dependence on Middle East crude, funded by a levy on oil wholesalers and trading firms that subsidises cargoes routed away from Hormuz, together with state support for pipelines in producing countries. The Global Gas Report 2026, from Snam and the International Gas Union, puts 2025 demand at a record 4,202 billion cubic metres and finds the loss of roughly 20% of global LNG supply hit markets less hard than the 2022 energy crisis, which it attributes to four years of investment in diversification, storage and regasification.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Energy and hydrocarbon feedstocks sit beneath most ACS cost structures, so the pattern matters more than any single figure. The gas report suggests the system has more absorption capacity than in 2022, which may limit the size of future price spikes. The UK cap increase shows that costs are still being passed through to households with a lag of several months. Japan's scheme is an example of a government paying to move supply away from a single chokepoint, a step other importers could copy and one that may gradually change freight patterns and landed costs in Asia. Considerations that follow include treating shipping risk in the strait as a persistent rather than temporary premium in logistics contracts, watching regulated energy prices in Europe as a lagging indicator for plant energy costs, and reviewing whether supply contracts allow the flexibility the wider gas market has built.

Lianhe Zaobao | MarketScreener | The Mainichi | Japan Today | La Repubblica

item.title: Trump said he has no timetable for Iran to return to talks, and the 24 August sanctions package set no deadline for countries to cut ties and named no large Chinese banks, which analysts say leaves Iran's main oil channel open.
item.description:
The pressure campaign is defined as much by what it leaves out as by what it covers. Trump said on 26 August that he is in no hurry to restart negotiations and set no deadline for Tehran, arguing that Washington holds the stronger position and that Iran faces high inflation and a deteriorating economy. The 24 August package announced by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent named about 60 people, companies and vessels and extended secondary sanctions — measures that penalise third parties for dealing with a sanctioned state — into digital assets, gold, aviation and shipping. It set no deadline for countries to stop trading with Iran, imposed no immediate penalties on those still doing so, and did not name the large Chinese financial institutions suspected of handling Iranian oil payments. Most Iranian oil that still moves goes to independent Chinese refiners in Shandong, known as teapots. Xu Muyu, a crude-oil analyst at the trade-intelligence firm Kpler, said Beijing has given no sign of directing them or Chinese banks to stop, and that this could change if Washington targeted major Chinese entities — a step that would risk raising tension before the September leaders' meeting (see the summit insight in this alert). Tehran has set out a two-year plan built on stockpiles of goods, foreign currency and gold plus energy rationing; its central bank says oil exports have almost stopped but that reserves remain accessible.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

For ACS producers the practical read is that the feedstock channel looks less disturbed than the announcement suggested, because the measures that would most affect oil flows have been held back. That defers the risk rather than removing it: if Washington later names large Chinese banks or sets firm deadlines, oil and petrochemical prices could move quickly, and companies exposed to both the US and Chinese markets would face a harder compliance position. Points that may be worth considering include keeping feedstock hedging and scenario ranges wide rather than narrowing them on the current calm, and continuing counterparty screening across Gulf, Chinese and Indian trade lanes, since designations have already reached intermediaries in several countries. The absence of a negotiating timetable suggests planning assumptions may need to allow for the disruption to persist rather than for an early settlement.

Cnyes | Beijing Daily | The Asahi Shimbun | South China Morning Post | Al Jazeera | The Diplomat | The Mainichi

item.title: Trump declared a 50% tariff on Canadian vehicles, parts and trucks from January 2027 and the White House is discussing further penalties, with both governments now preparing for a dispute that could last past the US midterm elections.
item.description:
The argument moved from goods to vehicles. On 24 August Trump said tariffs on cars, auto parts and trucks from Canada will rise to 50% from 1 January 2027. That sits on top of the 50% duties on about USD 20 billion of Canadian goods that took effect on 22 August under Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act, a rarely used clause allowing the president to penalise countries judged to discriminate against US commerce. A White House official said additional measures, including higher tariffs, are under discussion following Ottawa's dollar-for-dollar response. Officials on both sides indicate they are preparing for a dispute that could last past the US midterm elections, and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer publicly rejected Canada's account that late American demands broke the talks. Carmakers are the most exposed: Ford, General Motors, Stellantis, Toyota and Honda build high-volume models such as the F-Series Super Duty using components that cross the border, and a parts levy would reach across the North American supply chain. The four-month gap before January leaves room for a settlement. Canadian crude equals close to a fifth of total US petroleum consumption, and Canada also supplies aluminium and potash.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

North America is a core market for the Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) sector, and vehicle assembly is one of its larger end-markets, so the January date puts a defined deadline on that exposure. If the vehicle and parts tariffs take effect, they may raise the delivered cost of vehicles and components crossing the border, which could reduce build volumes and, with them, demand for structural adhesives, sealants and coatings on both sides. Canada's counter-duties, which cover pulp and paper, appliances, machinery and building inputs, may work the same way in the other direction. Things to consider over the next four months include mapping which product lines sit on either tariff list, reviewing where contracts allow cost pass-through, and testing whether routings that avoid the border are practical. The dependence figures cut both ways and could support a settlement, so scenario planning that allows for a deal as well as for escalation may be more useful than planning for a single outcome.

MarketScreener | Financial Post | LiveMint | CBC | Politico | AP | The Boston Globe
